title: How the Internet Works
subtitle: Packets, addressing, name resolution, and transport from browser to server
objectives: Explain what actually happens when you open a website
Describe how packets, IP addresses, and DNS get data to the right place
Trace a request from your browser to a server and back
Tell the difference between TCP and UDP and when each is used

lessons.title: Packets move through a network of routers

fieldTask.notice: Each numbered line is a router that answered along the measured path. Your count may be lower or higher than 10–20, and `*` means that hop did not answer the probe—not that no router exists there.

exercises.title: Routers pass your data toward its destination one hop at a time
exercises.body: When you open a website, the data is split into small chunks called *packets*. Each packet carries a destination IP address. Your router sends it to another router that knows a closer route; that router does the same. After roughly 10–20 hops, the packet reaches the server.
exercises.note: No router needs a complete map of the internet. It only needs to choose a useful next hop, so traffic can route around a failed link.

exercises.prompt: A router on the current path stops forwarding packets. Reroute the request through a healthy router and observe whether it reaches the server.
exercises.afterStatus: DELIVERED · 1 of 1 responses returned through the alternate router
exercises.why: Internet routing does not reserve one permanent end-to-end wire. When routing protocols advertise a healthy alternate path, later packets can traverse different routers and still reach the same destination IP.

exercises.prompt: You open a website. Roughly how many separate computers might your request pass through before it reaches the server?
exercises.why: Internet traffic commonly crosses 10–20 routers because each router forwards the packet across one segment of the route toward the destination. The exact hop count depends on network topology and routing policy.

exercises.prompt: Data doesn't travel as one big blob. It's broken into small chunks called ______.
exercises.why: A packet is a bounded chunk of data with addressing and control information. Splitting a message into packets lets routers forward each chunk independently; the receiver then reconstructs the original byte stream.

exercises.prompt: A router is forwarding a packet across the internet. Which field tells it the packet's network-layer destination?
exercises.why: A destination Internet Protocol (IP) address identifies a network-layer endpoint, usually an interface, for packet delivery. Routers use its network prefix to choose a next hop. It is not a physical location: addresses can change, one device can have several, and Network Address Translation can let many devices share one public address.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece to what it does.

pairs.right: A small chunk of your data
A logical source or destination for IP packets

exercises.why: A packet carries a chunk of data, an IP address names a logical network-layer source or destination, and a router forwards packets toward the destination prefix. An address identifies a network interface; it does not encode the device's physical location.

exercises.prompt: Build the packet's path from your laptop toward a website. Each router chooses only the next hop; the final component owns the destination address.
exercises.why: The laptop sends the packet to its local gateway, transit routers forward it toward the destination prefix, and the web server receives it at the addressed endpoint. No central machine chooses the whole path; if a router or link fails, packets may be dropped until routing converges on an alternate next hop.

exercises.title: DNS turns a domain name into an IP address
exercises.body: People type `google.com`, but routers need a numeric IP address. Before the browser connects, it asks the Domain Name System (DNS) for the IP linked to that name. DNS returns the number; the browser can then send packets toward it.
exercises.note: A name can keep working while its IP changes. That lets a service replace servers or direct users to a nearby location without teaching users a new address.

exercises.prompt: A browser in London resolves `shop.example` to a Virginia service. Change the DNS answer to the London service address.
choiceFeedback: Server CPU does not shorten the approximately 80ms network round trip.
The new DNS answer sends future connections to the nearby deployment.
A longer TTL keeps clients on the distant address for longer.
exercises.result: DNS directed the new connection to a nearby deployment
exercises.why: DNS can return different service addresses based on routing policy or resolver location. Existing cached answers remain until their TTL expires, so a DNS change does not move every client immediately.

exercises.prompt: You type `google.com`, but computers route by IP address. Who turns the name into the number?
exercises.why: The Domain Name System (DNS) resolves a domain name such as `google.com` to records that can include IP addresses. The browser uses a returned address to open a connection to the destination service.

exercises.prompt: DNS returns `A 203.0.113.8` and `AAAA 2001:db8::8` for one name. What did the two records provide?
choices: An IPv4 address and an IPv6 address
A primary server and a backup server
A port number and a password
exercises.why: A DNS `A` record carries an Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address, while an `AAAA` record carries an Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) address. A client can try a returned address when opening its connection; neither record promises a physical location or backup role.

exercises.prompt: Put a DNS lookup in order (simplified).
steps: Browser and operating system check their valid DNS caches
If not cached, ask a DNS resolver
exercises.why: The browser needs an address, but it checks browser and operating-system caches before sending a resolver query. On a miss, a resolver obtains the record and returns an IP address; each cached record remains usable only for its time to live (TTL).

exercises.prompt: In October 2016, a company called Dyn was attacked. Suddenly Twitter, Spotify, Reddit, and Netflix all went dark at once — even though those companies were fine. What had been knocked out?
exercises.why: Dyn provided authoritative DNS service for the affected domains. When those DNS answers became unavailable, clients could not discover the sites’ IP addresses even though the application servers were healthy; independent authoritative providers reduce this shared failure risk.

exercises.prompt: Why does DNS cache results instead of looking up every time? Select all that apply.
choices: Lookups take time — caching makes pages load faster
It reduces load on DNS servers
It makes the answer more accurate
The same names are requested over and over
exercises.why: A cached DNS record avoids repeated resolver round trips and reduces query load when many clients request the same name. Caching can return an older address until the record’s time to live expires, so it improves latency and capacity without guaranteeing freshness.

exercises.prompt: Build the two separate exchanges on a cache miss: the browser asks a resolver, the resolver obtains the authoritative answer, and the browser then connects directly to the web server.
exercises.why: The browser asks a resolver, which obtains the domain's record from authoritative DNS when no cache can answer. The browser receives the IP address and then opens a separate connection to the web server; DNS never forwards the HTTP request.

exercises.title: A page load is a chain of dependent network steps
exercises.body: On a fresh visit without cached DNS or a reusable connection, the browser resolves the name, opens a connection, completes TLS for HTTPS, sends the HTTP request, receives the response, and renders it. Cached results and existing connections can skip earlier steps.
exercises.note: A fresh HTTPS visit may spend separate round trips on DNS, the TCP connection, and TLS encryption before the browser requests the page itself.

exercises.prompt: Before your browser can send an HTTP request to a server, what does it need first?
exercises.why: An HTTP connection needs a routable destination. When the URL contains a domain name, DNS supplies an IP address before the browser can send packets toward the server.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when you visit `example.com`.
steps: DNS resolves `example.com` to an IP address
Browser opens a connection to that IP
Server sends back an HTTP response
exercises.why: DNS resolution supplies the destination IP, the browser opens a connection, and HTTP carries the request and response over that connection. Server processing must finish before the response can be returned and rendered.

exercises.prompt: Complete the separate lookup leg. The browser asks one service for an address, then connects directly to the web server.
exercises.why: The browser first exchanges a lookup with the Domain Name System (DNS), then uses a returned IP address to connect directly to the web server. Web traffic does not pass through DNS; the two edges represent separate network exchanges.

exercises.prompt: A user has a 70ms round trip to the origin server and a 10ms round trip to a nearby edge server. Which change directly reduces the network-latency floor?
choices: Serve the response from the nearby edge without an origin round trip
Give the distant origin more CPU cores
exercises.why: Serving from the nearby edge reduces round-trip time from 70ms to 10ms because packets traverse a shorter network path and do not continue to the origin. Faster application code can reduce processing time, but it cannot reduce the propagation portion of this measured network path.

exercises.prompt: Your page felt slow. The server responded in 5ms, but the total was 300ms. Where did the time most likely go?
exercises.why: Server processing accounts for 5ms of the 300ms total, leaving about 295ms elsewhere in the request path. Network round trips are therefore the dominant measured component under the stated timings.

exercises.prompt: Build the first uncached HTTPS visit after the browser receives a URL. Put the network-dependent steps in the order that makes the HTTP request possible.
exercises.why: On a fresh HTTPS visit, DNS supplies an address, transport establishes communication, TLS authenticates and encrypts the connection, and HTTP then carries the application request. Caches, connection reuse, and newer protocols can combine or skip work, but none can send the request before a usable secure path exists.

lessons.title: TCP and UDP: different transport guarantees

exercises.title: TCP repairs missing or out-of-order data; UDP leaves that choice to the app
exercises.body: IP can lose packets or deliver them out of order. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) detects gaps, retransmits missing data, and gives the application an ordered byte stream. User Datagram Protocol (UDP) sends independent messages without providing those guarantees.
exercises.note: Protocols can build reliability above UDP. HTTP/3 uses reliable QUIC streams over UDP, while HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 normally use TCP.

exercises.prompt: Which transport directly presents an application with a reliable, ordered byte stream?
exercises.why: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) numbers bytes, acknowledges received data, retransmits losses, and directly presents the application with an ordered byte stream. Bare UDP provides independent datagrams instead; protocols such as QUIC can build reliable streams above UDP.

exercises.prompt: An application wants independent messages and will decide for itself whether any missing message is still worth retrying. Which bare transport fits?
exercises.why: User Datagram Protocol (UDP) exposes independent datagrams without transport-level retransmission or ordering. That lets the application decide whether to ignore, retry, or add its own ordering for each message; it does not make every UDP-based application unreliable.

exercises.prompt: Match each transport statement to the mechanism it describes.

pairs.right: Independent datagrams; no delivery or order guarantee
Reliable QUIC streams carried over UDP
Uses UDP or TCP as the response and operation require

exercises.why: TCP directly supplies a reliable, ordered byte stream. UDP exposes independent datagrams without delivery or ordering guarantees. An application-layer transport can add those mechanisms over UDP; QUIC does this for HTTP/3. Classic DNS commonly uses UDP for ordinary queries and TCP when needed; encrypted DNS can instead travel over protocols such as HTTPS or TLS.

exercises.prompt: You're designing a multiplayer game's networking. Slide toward what you'd prioritize for player-movement updates.
exercises.rightLabel: Let new state supersede old (bare UDP)
exercises.why: Player positions are superseded by frequent newer updates. UDP avoids transport-level retransmission and ordered delivery of obsolete positions, reducing delay when occasional packet loss is acceptable.

exercises.prompt: Bare UDP does not retransmit missing data or restore order; those choices are left to the ______.
choices: application or protocol built above it
exercises.why: User Datagram Protocol (UDP) exposes independent datagrams without transport-level retransmission or ordering. An application can accept loss, retry selected data, or use a protocol such as QUIC that implements reliable streams above UDP; UDP alone does not guarantee that an application is faster.

exercises.prompt: You've now traced a request end to end. Which statement best captures how the internet moves your data?
choices: One connection sends the whole file at once with no addressing
Data is split into packets, addressed by IP, routed hop-by-hop, and reassembled
A central server copies data directly to your screen
The browser stores everything locally and never contacts a server
exercises.why: The sender divides data into packets addressed to an IP destination, routers forward them hop by hop, and the receiver reconstructs the application data. TCP adds reliable ordered delivery; UDP exposes independent datagrams with fewer guarantees.

exercises.prompt: Packet 2 is lost while TCP is carrying an ordered byte stream. Build the recovery path that lets the receiving application observe bytes 1, 2, 3 in order.
exercises.why: TCP tracks byte sequence positions. When later data arrives across a gap, the receiver retains it while loss detection triggers retransmission; only after the missing bytes arrive can the ordered stream advance. This reliability also explains why loss can delay later bytes.

exercises.prompt: A multiplayer client still uses an old game-server IP after DNS changed. New players connect correctly. What explains the split?
choices: Cached DNS records have not reached their TTL
Routers permanently bind each player to one IP
The new server needs more RAM
exercises.why: Existing clients may reuse a cached DNS answer until its time to live expires, while clients without that cache receive the new address. DNS changes are therefore gradual rather than simultaneous.
